# EU public procurement of solar PV: the supply-chain and trade dimension

## 1. The scale of Chinese dominance in the EU solar-PV supply chain

**(A) Established facts.** China's share of every major solar-PV manufacturing stage exceeds 80%, and is highest upstream. The IEA's flagship *Solar PV Global Supply Chains* report (2022, data updated 2024) puts China above 80% across polysilicon, ingots, wafers, cells and modules; its *Advancing Clean Technology Manufacturing* (2024) reports China holds more than 80% of global module manufacturing capacity and 95% of wafer capacity. IEA-PVPS data show China's share of global polysilicon production rising from 86% (2022) to 92% (2023) and 94% (2024). On the demand side, the European Solar Manufacturing Council (ESMC) states China accounted for more than 95% of the EU's solar-panel imports by value in 2024; Bruegel cites the same >95% figure for 2022. By contrast, the IEA puts Europe's share of global PV manufacturing at roughly 1%.

Inverters are the partial exception: Europe retains significant domestic players (SMA, Fronius), but Chinese vendors dominate globally — Huawei and Sungrow held about 55% of the global inverter market in 2024 (Wood Mackenzie), and nine of the world's top ten inverter vendors are Chinese. SMA announced a restructuring of up to 1,100 jobs in November 2024.

## 2. Trade-defence posture: 2013–2018 measures and 2023–2026 developments

**(A) Established facts.** In December 2013 the EU imposed anti-dumping (AD) and anti-subsidy/countervailing (ASD/CVD) duties on Chinese solar cells and modules, using a minimum import price (MIP) plus a volume undertaking. Bruegel estimates the measures raised Chinese panel prices in Europe by an average of ~47% from August 2013. The measures were extended 18 months in March 2017 and lapsed on 3 September 2018 (confirmed in a European Parliament written answer).

The one live trade-defence dossier in the sector concerns **solar glass**, not panels. Following an expiry review opened in July 2025, the Commission repealed the AD duty (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2314) and the countervailing duty (Regulation (EU) 2026/2310) on Chinese solar glass on 21–22 October 2026, after more than 12 years. The Commission's stated reason is that "no Union industry exists" — the last two EU producers, GMB and AGC Glass Europe, had left the market.

**(B) Debated / contested.** There has been **no formal initiation** of a new AD/CVD investigation into Chinese modules or cells in 2023–2026. In 2025 ESMC, joined by 23 European PV organisations, publicly demanded stricter import controls and new trade-defence tools, claiming Chinese TOPCon modules are sold in Europe at €0.109/Wp — about 31% below the €0.159/Wp ESMC says is needed to cover production and shipping (a ~46% "dumping margin"). The Commission has signalled it does not intend to impose trade restrictions on solar, and Germany has separately been reported to be weighing national barriers. These are proposals and signals, not enacted measures.

## 3. The Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR) and public procurement

**(A) Established facts.** The FSR (Regulation (EU) 2022/2560) applies since 12 July 2023, with mandatory notification in public procurement since 12 October 2023. Bidders must notify foreign financial contributions (FFCs) where the contract is worth at least €250 million and the bidder received at least €4 million in FFCs per non-EU country over the prior three years.

The first-ever FSR in-depth investigation (February 2024) targeted Chinese state-owned train-maker CRRC in a Bulgarian tender; CRRC withdrew. The solar sector followed: on 3 April 2024 the Commission opened two in-depth investigations into Chinese bidders for the 454.97 MW Rovinari photovoltaic park in Romania (partly financed by the EU Modernisation Fund) — the LONGi Solar Technologie/ENEVO consortium and two Shanghai Electric entities. Both withdrew in May 2024, and the Commission closed the probes without imposing remedies. Separately, in April 2024 the Commission opened its first *ex officio* FSR investigation, into Chinese wind-turbine suppliers.

**(B) Assessment / debate.** No FSR duties have yet been imposed in solar; the instrument's effect has been deterrent — Chinese bidders withdrew rather than face scrutiny. Analysts (Cleary, Taylor Wessing, Stibbe) read this as proof the FSR is reshaping Chinese participation in large EU tenders, though some argue it has yet to deliver substantive remedies. The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU criticised the probes as introducing uncertainty into tenders.

## 4. The European Solar Charter and the "Made in Europe" procurement debate

**(A) Established facts.** The European Solar Charter was signed on 15 April 2024 by 23 EU member states, the Commission and industry. It commits signatories to voluntary actions: accelerated permitting for manufacturing and deployment, "ambitious non-price criteria" in public procurement and renewable-energy auctions, and access to EU funding (Recovery and Resilience Facility, Innovation Fund). It is explicitly framed as early implementation of the Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA).

The NZIA (in force since June 2024) sets a benchmark that EU manufacturing meet 40% of annual deployment needs by 2030, and the European Solar PV Industry Alliance (ESIA) targets 30 GW of manufacturing capacity across the value chain by 2030 (requiring ~€30bn investment, per SolarPower Europe). From 30 December 2025, an NZIA implementing act requires member states to apply non-price criteria (sustainability and resilience) to at least 30% of annual renewable-auction volume (or 6 GW); the Commission published guidance in July 2026.

**(B) Debated.** The Charter stops short of quotas or explicit price preferences for EU-made modules, relying instead on "non-price" resilience criteria — a deliberate compromise. ESMC and manufacturers argue these are too weak and slow to compete with Chinese pricing; SolarPower Europe and deployment-focused firms warn that mandatory "Made in Europe" shares or tariffs would slow the energy transition and raise costs for public bodies and consumers.

## 5. The central tension: cheap imports vs strategic autonomy

**(A) The conflict.** Chinese panels are dramatically cheaper, letting public bodies and taxpayers decarbonise faster. ESMC's own figures illustrate the gap: imported Chinese modules at €0.109/Wp versus an estimated €0.159/Wp sustainable European price. Reshoring therefore means materially higher procurement costs and slower deployment.

**(B) Actor positions (attributed).**
- **Manufacturers (ESMC, Meyer Burger):** demand trade defence, "resilience" procurement preferences, and forced-labour-linked import controls to level the playing field.
- **SolarPower Europe (broad value chain, incl. installers/EPCs):** explicitly opposes trade-defence measures ("There must be no trade defence measures on solar PV products entering Europe", echoed by 420+ organisations under #MakeSolarEU), but endorses non-price resilience criteria and "European preference provisions where appropriate for strategic sectors".
- **European Commission:** has signalled no appetite for new solar trade restrictions, favouring the FSR and non-price criteria.
- **Member states:** split — Germany has floated national trade barriers; others prioritise cheap deployment.
- **NGOs / human-rights groups:** focus on forced labour in Xinjiang polysilicon rather than prices; the EU Forced Labour Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, applying from 14 December 2027) will ban products linked to forced labour, with polysilicon seen as the highest-risk input.
- **Trade unions:** support local manufacturing to protect jobs.

The core disagreement is whether resilience is best served by restricting imports (risk of higher prices and retaliation) or by demand-side support and diversification (Slower, costlier build-out of EU capacity).

## 6. Key data points: capacity vs demand, closures, NZIA/ESIA targets

**(A) Established facts.**
- **Demand:** the EU installed a record ~65.5 GW in 2024; SolarPower Europe projects ~65.1 GW in 2025 — the first market contraction in nearly a decade.
- **Supply:** Europe holds only ~1% of global PV manufacturing capacity (IEA), far below demand; the gap is met almost entirely by Chinese imports.
- **Factory closures:** Meyer Burger announced closure of its Freiberg, Germany module plant in early 2024 and a pivot to the US, then reversed course in August 2024 (cancelling a Colorado cell plant); its German subsidiaries filed for insolvency in 2025, and its US arm filed for Chapter 11 in June 2025 — widely cited as the emblematic failure of European PV manufacturing under Chinese price pressure. In solar glass, the last two EU producers (GMB, AGC Glass Europe) exited, prompting the 2026 duty repeal.
- **Targets:** NZIA 40% of deployment needs and ESIA's 30 GW manufacturing capacity by 2030.

**(B) Contested.** Analysts dispute whether the 30 GW/40% goals are achievable — Bruegel and others note that even if all announced projects materialise, Europe's cost disadvantage persists, and SolarPower Europe warns industrial-policy roll-out has been too slow to reverse factory closures.

---

## Sources

1. IEA, *Solar PV Global Supply Chains* (2022, updated) — https://www.iea.org/reports/solar-pv-global-supply-chains/executive-summary — accessed 2026-11-25.
2. IEA, *Advancing Clean Technology Manufacturing* (2024) — https://iea.org/reports/advancing-clean-technology-manufacturing/executive-summary — accessed 2026-11-25.
3. IEA-PVPS, *Trends in Photovoltaic Applications 2025* — https://iea-pvps.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/IEA-PVPS_Trends_2025-.pdf — accessed 2026-11-25.
4. ESMC, "Level Playing Field" — https://esmc.solar/level-playing-field — accessed 2026-11-25.
5. Bruegel, *Smarter European Union industrial policy for solar panels* — https://bruegel.org/policy-brief/smarter-european-union-industrial-policy-solar-panels — accessed 2026-11-25.

7. European Parliament, written answer on expiry of solar measures (2018) — https://europarl.europa.eu/RegData/questions/reponses_qe/2018/004503/P8_RE(2018)004503_EN.pdf — accessed 2026-11-25.
8. PV Magazine, "EU ends MIP against Chinese solar imports" (2018) — https://pv-magazine.com/2018/08/31/eu-ends-mip-against-chinese — accessed 2026-11-25.
9. EUR-Lex, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2314 (solar glass AD repeal) — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2026/2314/oj — accessed 2026-11-25.
